newsitem.title: UK: Juppe says France is "key" to monetary union.
newsitem.headline: Juppe says France is "key" to monetary union.

text.p: French Prime Minister Alain Juppe said in an interview published on Monday that France was the key to European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) and would meet the 1999 timetable for the launch of a single currency.
In an interview with the Financial Times newspaper, Juppe said: "I think France is the key. If France is not ready in time (to enter EMU in 1999) there will be no EMU for a long period."
Juppe criticised German demands for a tough stability pact for the single currency, which would set financial penalties for countries whose deficits overshot agreed limits.

"There seems to be some fear among some Germans that the Euro will be less good than the D-Mark, so they desire safeguards everywhere," Juppe said. "I think this should be settled through confidence-building measures, not over-rigid mechanisms."

In what the Financial Times described as a "foretaste" of President Jacques Chirac's position at Monday's Nuremberg summit with German Chancellor Helmut Kohl, Juppe also called for politicians to have some influence over the planned European Central Bank (ECB).

"The basis of the French position is that we don't want all decisions on economic, budgetary, fiscal and monetary policy to be shaped by a technocratic, automatic system under the sole authority of the ECB," he said. "That is not our concept of democracy."
He said the political leaders of member states should meet "periodically to fix broad lines of economic policy, dialogue with the central bank and give their opinion."
One element of this "political power," which is resisted by the Germans, would be to influence the exchange rate policy for the euro.

Juppe strongly rejected recent suggestions by former French President Giscard d'Estaing that the franc should be devalued agasint the mark, and said he himself had drawn attention to the dollar's undervaluation against the French currency.
Despite his unprecedented levels of unpopularity in France, Juppe stood by the planks of his economic policy.

"Inflation has been mastered, foreign trade is recording remarkable surpluses, the franc is stable, interest rates have come down faster than they have ever done in so short a time" and were now on a par with Germany's, Juppe said.
"People's purchasing power, contrary to what they think, is rising, not falling, and consumption is holding up well. Our growth target for next year of 2.3 to 2.4 percent should be met."
